"But one thing the facts cry out, and it can be clear, as they say, even to a blind man, that often through the translator's clumsiness or inattention the Greek has been wrongly rendered; often the original meaning of the sentence has been lost; often it has been necessary to choose among several possible meanings, and then only one has been translated, the translator either not understanding or not being able to reproduce in the target language the richness and depth of the original; often the translator has been biased, and instead of translating he has explained, and thus distorted; often he has been over-anxious to make the author intelligible, and in so doing has made him out to say something which he does not say, and, what is worse, something which he does not mean; often he has been over-anxious to be elegant, and in so doing has sacrificed faithfulness; often he has been over-anxious to be concise, and in so doing has sacrificed fullness; often he has been over-anxious to be clear, and in so doing has sacrificed precision; often he has sacrificed something to something else. These are the facts. And therefore I say that the Greek text should be published together with the translation, so that those who know Greek may see how the translator has translated, and where he has failed to reproduce the original, and where he has sacrificed something to something else. And those who do not know Greek will still be able to see that the translator has not translated the whole of the original, and where he has failed to reproduce the original, and where he has sacrificed something to something else."
